title: No Verified Case, No License for Vietnam’s Dog Meat Trade
excerpt: No documented incident is available here to support trade defenses. Public safety still demands traceability, quarantine, and a national abolition law.
body_html:
A stolen pet, poison-bait seizure, or court conviction can expose cruelty in concrete terms. None is documented in the material available for this dispatch. Publishing an invented arrest, victim, location, or disease event would betray families, animals, and readers.

Myths need records, not slogans

“Tradition” cannot excuse theft, illegal transport, quarantine evasion, or unsafe slaughter. “Farm-raised dogs” cannot be treated as proof that every animal in trade comes from lawful, traceable production. Each claim requires records: origin, ownership, veterinary inspection, transport permits, quarantine compliance, and enforcement outcomes.

No verified source is supplied here proving that dog farms do not exist, nor proving that all traded dogs come from stolen homes. That narrower statement matters. Evidence must identify which animals were stolen, which shipments violated rules, and which agencies acted. Moral urgency cannot replace proof.

Public health still demands precision

Rabies transmission generally involves infected saliva entering bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. After possible exposure, wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical assessment. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. WHO guidance explains this response.

Household exposure incidents and commercial supply chains are separate dimensions of biosecurity. One does not prove the other. Both require transparent reporting, veterinary oversight, and accountable enforcement.

Vietnamese leadership needs a clear legal demand

Vietnamese families, pet guardians, veterinarians, and local reformers can demand records instead of rumors: public seizure reports, quarantine data, ownership investigations, and prosecution outcomes. SDE’s campaign demand is distinct from any official public-health target: complete abolition of the dog meat trade nationwide by 2030.

Sign the national petition. Add your name to a public demand for abolition by 2030, transparent enforcement, and protection for families and animals.

Rabies control cannot stop at household gates—but campaign claims cannot outrun evidence.

No verified seizure, arrest, conviction, location, or official dataset is available in the material supporting this post. That means no invented victim, raid, poison incident, or disease link. Families and animals deserve better than rumor dressed as investigation.

Trade defenses such as “tradition” or “farm-raised dogs” need records. Where did each animal come from? Who owned it? Did transport follow permits and quarantine rules? Was slaughter inspected? Without traceability, enforcement cannot distinguish lawful activity from theft, illegal transport, or regulatory breach.

Rabies remains a separate public-health concern. Infected saliva can transmit rabies through bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. After possible exposure, wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical care. Post-exposure vaccination and indicated immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies must occur before symptoms develop. Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal.

Vietnamese communities can demand transparent records, stronger enforcement, and complete abolition of the dog meat trade by 2030.
